profile.reading:
Lumen Albany 4 is a network colocation site at 10 Airline Drive in the Town of Colonie, in the Albany metropolitan area of New York, mapped here as a point rather than a building outline. It is not a hyperscale campus and should not be read as one. Lumen Technologies, formerly CenturyLink, which took the Lumen name on September 14, 2020 and the LUMN ticker four days later, and which absorbed Level 3 Communications in a deal that closed November 1, 2017, sells this class of site as carrier neutral edge colocation attached to its own long haul network. Lumen's published colocation material describes more than 175 such facilities across more than 60 North American markets and quotes cabinet power in a 3 to 15 kilowatt band that varies by site. It publishes no square footage, no total megawatt figure and no individual street address for any of them, which is why the facility code Albany 4 is the most specific identifier available.

The local property record is worth reporting because of what it does not contain. The Town of Colonie assessment roll lists parcels at 4, 6, 8, 10A, 10B, 10C, 11, 12, 12A and 13 Airline Drive, under owners including a private realty group, an office trust and a school district body, but no parcel numbered simply 10, and no parcel on that street owned by Lumen, CenturyLink or Level 3. The Lumen group appears in the roll only in the sections for network property, as special franchise parcel 99.55-6-11 in property class 866 for telephone, assessed at 575,338 dollars under the name Level 3 Telecom NY care of the CenturyLink property tax department in Broomfield, Colorado, and in the utility and railroad section as class 836 telecommunications equipment described as outside plant and fiber optic cable spread across the South Colonie, North Colonie, Niskayuna and Mohonasen school districts. The straightforward reading is that Lumen occupies leased space in a building it does not own and pays tax on its network plant rather than on real property here. Which of the Airline Drive parcels holds the suite is not established, so no owner, improvement square footage or year built is recorded on this page.

New York's regulatory posture toward data centers changed sharply in 2026, and the interesting question for a site like this one is whether any of it reaches it. Executive Order 62, signed July 14, 2026, defines a data center as a facility that consumes or can consume 50 megawatts or more, directs the Department of Environmental Conservation to hold incomplete permit applications for such facilities in abeyance, and runs until the Department of Public Service delivers a final generic environmental impact statement, with carve outs for manufacturing, research, education, medical uses and the Empire AI consortium. A colocation site quoting cabinet power in kilowatts is almost certainly far below that line. The Responsible Data Center Development Act, passed by the legislature on June 4, 2026, uses much lower thresholds, including renewable procurement duties at a 5 megawatt peak load and host community benefit funding for existing facilities adding 20 megawatts or more. Whether this site clears 5 megawatts cannot be answered from the public record, because Lumen does not publish the number. Meanwhile NYISO logged 51 large data load interconnection requests statewide in 2026 against six in 2022, and in Albany itself a proposal by Guild Ventures for a mixed use campus on the 76 acre Kenwood Commons site in the South End, with a data center component drawing up to 100 megawatts, has the city's Common Council weighing zoning rules for a use the code does not currently name.

profile.capacity_note: Nothing here fixes any of the four power quantities. it_capacity_mw is absent because Lumen publishes no IT load for any of its colocation sites. utility_power_mw is absent because no National Grid or New York Public Service Commission filing reviewed here names a service level for this address. No standby diesel rating and no on site generation are published. The only Lumen power figure available is a company wide cabinet range of 3 to 15 kilowatts that the data sheet says varies by site, which is a range across a fleet of more than 175 buildings and cannot be converted into a facility total.
profile.research_note: Facility page rebuilt 2026-09-05. Lumen publishes no per building square footage, megawatt figure or street address for any colocation site, so no power or space key is written. Occupancy rather than ownership is inferred from the Town of Colonie assessment roll, which carries the Lumen group only as special franchise and outside plant assessments and shows no fee owned parcel on Airline Drive.
profile.community_note: The Albany area is contesting data center growth around this site rather than at it. Guild Ventures has proposed a multibillion dollar mixed use technology campus on the 76 acre Kenwood Commons site in Albany's South End, with a data center component that could draw up to 100 megawatts, and the city's Common Council has been weighing zoning rules because Albany's code contains no data center category. NYISO recorded 51 large data load project requests statewide in 2026 against six in 2022. No community objection, hearing record or local approval proceeding specific to this Colonie colocation site was found.
profile.regulatory_note: Two New York measures now shape the market this site sits in, and both turn on thresholds this facility has never been shown to cross. Executive Order 62, signed July 14, 2026, applies to data centers that consume or can consume 50 megawatts or more, holds incomplete Department of Environmental Conservation permit applications in abeyance, and directs the Department of Public Service to run a generic environmental impact statement process, to convene a data center interconnection working group within 60 days and to report on transmission owner practices within 90 days, with the Department of Environmental Conservation to assess water withdrawal rules within twelve months and Empire State Development to build a community investment framework within 60 days. Facilities primarily used for manufacturing, research, education or medical care, and the Empire AI consortium, are excluded. The Responsible Data Center Development Act, passed June 4, 2026, would reach much smaller loads, requiring facilities at or above a 5 megawatt peak to source at least a third of their electricity from renewables by 2030 with higher shares later, setting efficiency goals through NYSERDA, and requiring host community benefit funding from existing facilities that add 20 megawatts or more.

reading.body:
Lumen Albany 4 is a network colocation site in Colonie, New York, occupied by Lumen Technologies but not owned by it. Lumen publishes no power consumption figure for this or any of its more than 175 colocation sites, quoting only a cabinet-level range of 3 to 15 kilowatts that varies across the fleet. The facility code Albany 4 is the most specific public identifier available. The local property record shows Lumen holds only network plant and franchise assessments on this street, with no identified building owner or square footage, so no independent estimate of power draw can be made from town records.

New York's regulatory environment shifted sharply in 2026 with two measures that turn on thresholds this site's published record does not reach. Executive Order 62, signed July 14, 2026, applies only to facilities that consume or can consume 50 megawatts or more. The Responsible Data Center Development Act, passed June 4, 2026, sets renewable procurement duties at 5 megawatts peak load and requires host community benefit funding for existing sites adding 20 megawatts or more. Whether Albany 4 crosses the 5 megawatt line cannot be determined from the public record.

This site ranks second among the one facility in New York with published megawatt capacity, a ranking that reflects only that the state's data center capacity is almost entirely undisclosed. The Albany metro area is experiencing sharp growth in data load interconnection requests, with NYISO recording 51 large data load projects statewide in 2026 against six in 2022, and the city of Albany is drafting zoning rules around a proposed 100 megawatt mixed use campus nearby. Whether this colocation site will participate in that growth or remain a small carrier-neutral facility cannot be read from the specifications available.
